consensus_summary: The ship primarily symbolizes the Church as the vessel of salvation (Noah's ark typology, Gospel storm-calming and fishing boats as the barque of Peter, architectural 'nave') that carries believers through the sea/world; secondary alternatives include the individual faith journey and ships as emblems of worldly commerce, pride, or wealth (Tarshish, Tyre, Babylon).
book_summary: The ship is an earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding the sea of peoples, with rulers as pilots, inhabitants as crew, armies as defenders, and wealth as cargo; Christ walks the sea without needing a vessel, and a ship may break while its people survive.
consensus_core_identification: the Church (salvific vessel carrying the faithful)
boundary_disagreement: Consensus treats Church as the settled primary (with commerce/pride as context-specific alternative); book excludes the Church entirely and generalizes the commercial/city-state imagery to any governed political entity.
material_contradiction: The same symbol cannot primarily be both the Church (spiritual body of salvation) and an earthly political body (temporal power that may be wrecked while people survive); accepting the book replaces the consensus referent.
rationale: Consensus cores (across all four responses) reduce to Church via ark typology, boat narratives, and tradition; the book core reduces to political body via the same prophetic ship-of-state passages the consensus lists only as secondary. These are incompatible central identifications, not a shared category with altered boundaries. The book's scriptures align with its political reading and omit the Church-supporting texts.
strongest_objection: Near-universal patristic, liturgical, and traditional Church-as-ship reading (supported by Noah typology and multiple Gospel boat scenes) is wholly displaced without engagement.
